events.title: C++ gains templates
events.summary: AT&T's Cfront 3.0 release was the first C++ compiler to support templates, enabling generic programming in production code.
events.about: Templates let you write one piece of code that works with many types — a single `sort()` for integers and strings, or one `vector` class instead of separate `IntVector` and `StringVector` copies. This idea became the foundation for C++'s standard library (`vector`, `map`, `sort`).

narrative.whyChosen: Before templates, C++ libraries were either copy-pasted for every data type or written with unsafe void pointers. Templates made reusable, type-safe libraries practical.
narrative.whyImportant: Developers could ship one generic [container] or algorithm and reuse it across their whole codebase — with no runtime performance penalty.
narrative.problemSolved: Every time you needed a list of a new type, you rewrote the same linked-list or sort logic from scratch. Templates let you write it once and instantiate it for any type.

events.title: Apple PowerBook released
events.summary: Apple introduced the PowerBook line in October 1991 — laptops with the keyboard pushed toward the screen hinge and a built-in trackball.
events.about: The PowerBook 100, 140, and 170 set the template for modern laptop ergonomics — palm rest, centered pointing device, and compact footprint. Mobile developers and writers carried Mac [OS] on the road; the line stayed Apple's portable platform until the MacBook era. Its industrial design influenced every laptop that followed.

narrative.whyChosen: The PowerBook defined the modern laptop layout that [PC] makers copied throughout the 1990s.
narrative.whyImportant: It made Macintosh development and publishing portable for creative professionals.
narrative.problemSolved: Early portables placed keyboards awkwardly; users needed a usable pointing device without external mice.
